blocks.x: In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

The historical epic is a staple of cinema, and it's currently proving to be one of the most popular genres. The 21st century's headline filmmaker Christopher Nolan delivered the most ambitious of its kind in recent memory with his adaptation of Homer's ancient Greek epic The Odyssey, which debuted this summer. Dubbed an "unrivaled cinematic spectacle" in Joe Schmidt's review for Collider, The Odyssey is likely to sweep up at the 2027 Academy Awards, and might even break the nominations record set by Ryan Coogler's Sinners this year.

Having made over $1.6 billion at the box office and still sailing towards new milestones, The Odyssey is far and away the biggest success in Nolan's filmography, and is also the highest-grossing historical epic of all time. Part of its success can be attributed to its star-studded ensemble, led by Matt Damon as the King of Ithaca, and including Lupita Nyong’o, Charlize Theron, Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Jon Bernthal, Zendaya, and Robert Pattinson.

The historical epic genre's biggest hit of all time is encouraging fans to seek other examples on streaming. One such example is The Last Samurai, the 2003 gem set in 1878 during the Meiji period in Japan. Hollywood veteran Tom Cruise stars in the film as Civil War veteran Captain Nathan Algren, as he joins forces with director Edward Zwick before the pair would make Jack Reacher: Never Go Back. Also starring Ken Watanabe, Hiroyuki Sanada, Timothy Spall, and others, The Last Samurai is a true hidden treasure in the historical epic genre and is currently one of the ten most-streamed movies on HBO Max in the U.S.

Five legends. Five completely different ways of getting out alive — with style, with muscle, with charm, with luck, or with a plan so intricate it probably shouldn't work. Ten questions will reveal which action hero was built to have your back.

CSomeone who keeps their nerve and their sense of humour when everything is falling apart.
DSomeone who knows the history of wherever we are and what we're walking into.
ESomeone with the right contact, the right cover identity, and the right exit already arranged.

You have to get somewhere dangerous, fast. How do you travel?
How you get there is half the mission.

AOn foot through terrain no one else would attempt — I move where vehicles can't follow.
BOn a motorcycle, a cargo plane, or anything else that gets me there before I think too hard about it.
CIn something that belongs to someone else — borrowed, stolen, or improvised under fire.
DFirst class, with a cover identity and a gadget that does something I won't explain until it's needed.
EBy whatever means are available — I've driven, flown, and once arrived by camel. The destination matters, not the method.

This is when you find out what someone is really made of.

APrecise and minimal — tell me what I need to know and nothing else. Every word has a cost.

CEnthusiastic and slightly chaotic — but always with useful information buried somewhere in the noise.
DCalm and controlled through an earpiece, with a plan that covers every variable I haven't thought of yet.
EBarely at all — silence is a language and they speak it fluently.

Who someone is when you need them most is the only thing that matters.

blocks.c: mgm-logo.jpg

ACome in alone, quietly, and get me out before anyone knows they were there.

A great partner fills the gap you didn't know you had.

ATechnology that shouldn't exist yet and the training to use it under any conditions.
BSurvival instinct so refined it borders on supernatural — and the scars to prove it's been tested.

DThe ability to walk into any room in the world and immediately become the most trusted person in it.
EStubbornness that refuses to accept a situation is hopeless — and the improvisational skill to back it up.

Every partnership has a cost. Which of these can you live with?
No one comes without baggage. The question is whether you can carry it together.

AA partner who never fully switches off — always watching exits, always calculating threats, even at dinner.
BA partner who gets the job done brilliantly but has the emotional availability of a locked filing cabinet.
